sm: The episode marks Friday the thirteenth by looking at the language of superstition. The host explains that phrases like bragging about a clean driving record can make people say don't jinx it, as if speaking could change the outcome. Merriam-Webster dates the noun jinx to 1902 and the verb to 1913, and says it might come from the name of a small woodpecker called the wryneck, though that origin is only a maybe. Early twentieth century baseball helped spread the word. The host then turns to theater, where saying the name Macbeth inside a playhouse is taboo, and people instead say the Scottish play or perform rituals like spinning, spitting, and knocking to be let back in. She notes that the word taboo entered English in 1777 through James Cook's writing about Pacific islands.

The host says taboo probably came from Tongan or Maori words and was reinforced by other Pacific languages. The Macbeth curse legend may be more modern than it seems, since the scholar Paul Menzer found no mention of it until around the 1930s, and in the eighteenth century a different play was said to be unlucky. The 1849 Astor Place riot in New York, with more than ten thousand people, is often cited as evidence, and the Royal Shakespeare Company suggests struggling theaters staged Macbeth to raise money. In hospitals, staff avoid saying the word quiet, but a 2019 study over sixty-one days and a narrative review found no real effect on workload, only on how busy people felt. Superstition as a word dates to the early 1300s, and its Latin root means to stand. The host concludes that such phrases help people handle uncertainty and that rituals may reduce anxiety rather than change fate.

This part wraps up the episode with a listener call from Molly, who describes the family word who buddy. Her daughter coined it just before turning three, on Halloween, while excitedly handing out candy and shouting that who buddy wants some candy. The family still uses it, for example when asking who buddy is ready for dinner or who buddy wants to pick the movie, and Molly hopes it lasts forever. The host, Mignon Fogarty, thanks her and says moms always want those adorable words to go on forever. She invites listeners to share their own family words using the phone number in the show notes. She also credits the production team for the show.
